title: A cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase-like scaffold organizes monoterpenoid indole alkaloid biosynthesis.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and read the 54-page supplementary PDF of the matching bioRxiv preprint (doi 10.64898/2026.04.16.718883, CC-BY-NC) and extracted its text. Counted every data table: Table S1 = 43 engineered yeast strains each with one product titer in mg per litre; Table S2 = 6 rows of enzyme kinetics (KM in micromolar, Vmax in nmol per mg of GS per minute, with 95% confidence intervals); Table S4 = 23 protein sequences in FASTA format (11 VinBLAST/CAD-like proteins, 3 geissoschizine synthase proteins, the rest are tags and reporters); Table S7 = a 7x7 percent-identity matrix; Table S8 = 8 plant genome sources. Also confirmed no PubMed Central full text, no GEO/SRA/BioProject links, no structures in the Protein Data Bank under this DOI or the name VinBLAST, and that the only deposited data are 9 GenBank cDNA accessions PV770557-PV770565.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The ~160 mg per litre catharanthine fed-batch titre and the ~1000-fold improvement claim; the relative in vitro activity values for VinBLAST-homolog x geissoschizine-synthase pairings, which appear only as bar charts in main Figure 5c and supplementary figures, not as a numeric table; the mass-spectrometry metabolite profiling and microscopy results, which are images only.

a1_downloadable.note: The Science article itself is paywalled with no PubMed Central copy, but the identical preprint and its full supplementary PDF download freely under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial licence; I opened both. Physical materials (strains, plasmids) need a materials transfer agreement, but no data does.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Product titre is literally a column in supplementary Table S1 ('Titer (mg l-1)'), and KM and Vmax are columns in Table S2. No construction needed - but see A5 for how few rows there are.

a3_inputs_present.note: Full amino-acid sequences for all 23 proteins are printed as FASTA text in Table S4, so no accession lookups are needed. Genotype strings in Table S1 name every genetic part.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are explicit everywhere I looked: mg l-1 for titres, micromolar for KM, nmol per mg GS per min for Vmax, with confidence intervals and the fitting software version named.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. Counted in the file: 43 strain-titre rows in Table S1 (and only ~15 of those differ in the protein variant rather than the host pathway), 6 kinetics rows in Table S2, 23 sequences in Table S4 of which 14 are pathway proteins, and roughly 24 enzyme-pair activity values that exist only as bars in a figure. The checklist needs ~1,500 labelled rows, or ~400 for classification; this is two orders of magnitude short no matter how the table is reshaped.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 3.2 MB supplementary PDF; the whole numeric dataset is well under 10 kB once typed out.
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small - but small for the wrong reason, which is exactly the A5 failure.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Table S1 plate-culture titres are consistent with the figures; the headline ~160 mg l-1 is the fed-batch value for strain CA02 (164.9 mg l-1 in the text) versus 9.93 mg l-1 for the same strain in 24-well plates, which the paper states clearly rather than conflating.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels are physical measurements: alkaloid titres by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry of yeast cultures, and kinetic constants from in vitro enzyme assays fitted to the Michaelis-Menten model. Nothing is another model's output. The only computational object is a homology structural model, used for mutant design, not as a label.

backbone.name: ESM-2, a protein language model (would have been the obvious choice for embedding the CAD-like sequences)
backbone.hardware: Not assessed - project died at Part A5 before backbone fit mattered.
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the paper's own data is Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial.

integration.partner_dataset: UniProt plus Pfam/InterPro could supply thousands of plant cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase (CAD) family sequences joinable to these 14 pathway proteins.
integration.join_key: UniProt accession / GenBank accession (PV770557-PV770565, AEO99200.1, W8JWW7.1 are present in Table S4).
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which members of the large plant CAD family act as protein scaffolds that organise alkaloid biosynthesis rather than as alcohol-reducing enzymes - a real question, but this paper supplies labels for only about eleven of them, so the partner resource would be unlabelled.

controls.positive_control: Strain GM02 (strictosidine beta-glucosidase deleted, titre drops to 0.01 mg l-1) and the interaction mutant VinBLAST M298E,V299E, which abolishes the boost - both are in Table S1 and would be the known effects any model must recover.
controls.negative_control: Not runnable at this size: with 43 rows, label shuffling cannot be distinguished from sampling noise.
controls.external_validation: None. The scaffolding-activity label for CAD-like proteins has, as far as I found, never been measured outside this paper, so there is no second dataset to test on.

honest_claim_h3: With 43 strain titres and roughly 24 enzyme-pair activity values, the only honest claim available would be a descriptive one about eleven specific proteins from eleven plant species that this one lab chose to test, not a predictive statement about the plant cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase family.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a plant protein's sequence to predict whether it boosts alkaloid production when added to an engineered yeast strain.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered: one row per protein, the input being the amino-acid sequence of a cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase-like (CAD-like) plant protein plus the identity of the partner enzyme it is paired with. Verified count of such proteins in the files: 11 CAD-like proteins and 3 partner enzymes, giving at most a few dozen pairings.
plain_idea.predict: How much more of a target alkaloid (geissoschizine methyl ether, catharanthine or vindoline) the yeast strain makes, measured as milligrams per litre by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, or the fold increase in enzyme rate from an in vitro assay.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Metabolic engineers building yeast factories for the anticancer drug vinblastine would want to know which scaffold protein to bolt in without testing each one by hand; even a failed model would map how far scaffolding activity spreads across the CAD family. But the data here cannot support either answer.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: embed the 11 CAD-like protein sequences with a protein language model and regress against the measured boost in alkaloid titre or enzyme rate, to predict which other plant CAD-family members would work as biosynthetic scaffolds. The idea is sound in principle and the data is clean, documented and in stated units - it is simply far too small, with 43 strain-titre rows and roughly 24 enzyme pairings, to fit or honestly evaluate any model.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: the entire numeric dataset is a few dozen rows typed out of a PDF, and embedding 23 short plant proteins with a small ESM-2 checkpoint is a couple of minutes of laptop CPU time.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in supplementary Table S1 and the sequences in Table S4. That took fifteen minutes and killed the project: 43 titres and 11 candidate scaffold proteins.

verdict_reason: Beautiful, clean, fully-unit-stated experimental data - and far too little of it. Verified in the supplementary PDF: 43 yeast strain titres, 6 kinetics rows, 11 candidate scaffold protein sequences, roughly 24 enzyme pairings that exist only as bar charts. A5 fails by roughly 30-fold; no accession-linked omics, structures or screens exist to enlarge it. The biology (a dehydrogenase repurposed as a scaffold that raises catharanthine to ~160 mg per litre) is genuinely exciting, which is precisely the trap - the finding is a discovery, not a dataset.
